newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine govt tells judge stands by labor decrees.
newsitem.headline: Argentine govt tells judge stands by labor decrees.

text.p: The Argentine government formally replied Friday to a judge who suspended President Carlos Menem's labor reform decrees, telling her it stood by their "legitimacy" despite trade union complaints.

Menem's attempts to tackle 17.3 percent unemployment by passing decrees making labor more flexible have tripped on court rulings -- responding to trade union petitions -- that they are unconstitutional and must be suspended.

But Labor Minister Armando Caro Figueroa replied to Labor Judge Ines Gassibe, who froze the decrees Monday pending a full explanation by the government, with a 107-page document declaring the "legitimacy of the decrees."

His ministry issued a statement defending Menem's decrees signed last December "on the grounds that they merely regulate collective negotiation" and insisting they respect norms of the Geneva-based International Labor Organization.
The Peronist government resorted to decrees in the face of opposition in Congress and a breakdown in negotiations with unions, who fear their power is under threat.
The CGT staged a 24-hour general strike on December 26, its third in the year.

The government was also working on another batch of decrees to follow the first three, which let workers choose their union health plan, let smaller firms bypass national unions in collective pay talks and let firms appeal to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis.

But two weeks ago, they were declared unconstitutional by Labor Judge Julio Garcia Martinez and shortly afterwards Gassibe ordered their suspension. The government has since threatened to have him impeached.

Menem argues it is vital to modernize Argentina's labor legislation -- much of which dates from the first government of Juan Domingo Peron in the 1940s -- to fight unemployment. Reforms are also demanded by international lending agencies, including the International Monetary Fund.
